« Pourquoi voulez-vous notre photo ? Nou: “Why do you want our photo? We’re just normal people.” That is precisely what makes their stories so beautiful.
L'homme aux dosas, Raymond, Robin, Jasme: The dosa man, Raymond, Robin, Jasmeet and Elias, Montrealers. Photo: Prajwala Dixit
Plus de 1,7 million de personnes vivent: More than 1.7 million people live in Montréal, a metropolis teeming with life. Some were born here, others chose to live here or were forced to. Whatever the reason people live here, they enrich their surroundings, shaping them over time. A stay in Montréal often begins and ends at Pierre Elliott Trudeau airport. As the days go by, you get around by taxi and eat at a wide variety of restaurants. That is how you get to know the city, its history and its culture: through the drivers and the staff of these eateries.
Au cours de ces conversations, les gens: Over the course of these conversations, people show us the historic churches where they were married and the places where they like to have a coffee, and they share their favourite spots with us. These exchanges, though brief, are powerful; they yield tender stories of love, loss and belonging, told in confidence. Here are five of them, narrated by Montrealers of few words.
Au cours du trajet entre la rue Marie-An: On the ride from Marie-Anne Street to the Jean-Talon Market, Raymond, in his booming voice, encourages his passengers to practise their French. “Go on, try,” he says. “Your French is better than my English!” In a conversation that mixes both languages, he tells the story of his arrival in Montréal three decades ago. In Haiti, he had an ordinary office job, punching the clock at work every day. “I prefer my job as a driver,” he admits.
Raymond, chauffeur de taxi. Photo: Prajw: Raymond, taxi driver. Photo: Prajwala Dixit
Les Canadiens d’origine haïtienne choisi: Canadians of Haitian origin have been choosing Montréal as their adopted home since the 1930s. Many first came as students and returned to Haiti after completing their studies in Canada. Their numbers grew exponentially in the 1970s, when the political climate forced many Haitians to migrate. Many of them, like Raymond, now work in low-paying jobs such as taxi driving, which is not spared by racism and discrimination.
Raymond ne nous dira pas ce qui l’a amen: Raymond won’t tell us what brought him to Montréal, expressing nothing but love for the city, which he says is home. “I feel good here,” he says. He flashes his biggest smile for the camera before saying goodbye to his passengers and wishing them a good day.
Direction rue Saint-Denis. La course com: Next stop: Saint-Denis Street. The ride begins with a warm welcome in Elias’s taxi. Expertly navigating the city’s streets, Elias has become a roving guide who tells the story of the city. But when we ask him whether Montréal is home, he answers with a sigh.
Elias, chauffeur de taxi. Photo: Prajwal: Elias, taxi driver. Photo: Prajwala Dixit
« Maintenant, ça l’est », dit-il. Dans u: “It is now,” he says. In another life, Elias worked for 10 years at an architecture firm in Dubai before settling in Beirut and starting his own business. While he was visiting his brother on Long Island, New York, civil war broke out in Lebanon.
C’était en avril 1975, et la guerre a du: That was in April 1975, and the war lasted until the early 1990s. During that time, more than a million people left the country and more than a hundred thousand lost their lives. With no way of going home once the war had broken out, Elias and his family were forced to seek refuge and rebuild their lives in Montréal. “I don’t like this place,” he says bluntly.
Vivre à Montréal a été un rappel constan: Living in Montréal has been a constant reminder of what he lost through no fault of his own. His qualifications were not recognized in the city. And with a family of three children (and now two grandchildren), he could not afford to go back to school to further his training. So he had no choice but to drive his taxi to earn a living. “For now, this is what I do,” he adds, a note of nostalgia in his voice.
Sur Sainte-Catherine, en plein centre-vi: On Sainte-Catherine Street, right downtown, the aromas of idlis, vadas and dosas waft out of a commercial building. In the small kitchen of Chennai Express, the head cook is busy making dosas, a delicacy served in every household in southern India. The dish and its accompaniments – sambar and chutney – are in high demand among the many customers looking for a quick, reasonably priced bite to fill them up
L'homme aux dosas, propriétaire du resta: The dosa man, owner of the Chennai Express restaurant. Photo: Prajwala Dixit
« Vous pouvez prendre une photo des <em>: “You can take a picture of the dosas if you want. Not of me, OK?” the restaurant’s owner tells us. The dosas sizzle in the pan, their white batter turning crisp and golden. The cook quickly adds a potato filling to the centre and sprinkles it with raw onion. With an expert hand, he folds the dosas into squares, lifts them out of the pan and packs them carefully, without forgetting the coconut chutney and the vegetable sambar.
« J’ai enseigné à McGill. Maintenant, je: “I taught at McGill. Now I run this restaurant,” he says, handing a plate of food to a customer. Our host is originally from Chennai, in the state of Tamil Nadu, India, a port city whose skyline is cut by the gopuras of temples, church steeples and the domes of mosques. His restaurant was the first to serve authentic South Indian food in downtown Montréal. It may not be a fancy place, but the food it serves gets a 10 out of 10.
« D’accord, vous pouvez prendre ma photo: “All right, you can take my picture. But I’m keeping my mask on, OK?” the owner of Chennai Express concedes. His name, however, remains a mystery. Like the superheroes known only by their work and their alias, he has earned the nickname “the dosa man” – and he wears it so well.
De retour sur le Plateau-Mont-Royal, rue: Back on the Plateau-Mont-Royal, on Gilford Street, we find ourselves at Palais Maharaja. The restaurant’s doors open onto a long dining room whose ceiling is adorned with a bamboo artwork. The dim lighting mingles with the rays of sunshine streaming in through a large open window, through which you can glimpse the traffic and pedestrians on Saint-Denis Street.
Robin et Jasmeet sont originaires du Pen: Robin and Jasmeet are from Punjab, India, where great minds and liberal thinkers flow together like the five rivers that cross the region. It is home to the Harmandir Sahib, the site of the highest spiritual significance for Sikhs. It is also home to delicious North Indian cuisine, with specialties such as chole bhature and tandoori chicken.
Jasmeet, chef cuisinnier et Robin, propr: Jasmeet, head cook, and Robin, owner of Palais Maharaja. Photo: Prajwala Dixit
Les Pendjabis sont connus pour leur natu: Punjabis are known for their sociable nature and their warmth. Robin’s love for his homeland shows not only in the dishes he serves, but also in the paintings and artwork that adorn the walls of his restaurant. “I opened the restaurant four years ago,” he says. It’s a hard industry to navigate, all the more so during a pandemic. His business survived thanks to the delivery services offered through various apps.
Robin est impassible, mais ses yeux parl: Robin’s face gives nothing away, but his eyes speak, hinting at the work and effort it has taken to keep a place like his running since 2018. He and his head cook, Jasmeet Singh, would rather serve their customers than talk about their personal journeys. Jasmeet, who is especially shy, says nothing. He nods politely and simply smiles when complimented on his cooking. He expresses himself through the dishes he makes for Palais Maharaja’s customers. All it takes is one bite of his piping-hot kulcha, with The Kapil Sharma Show playing in the background, to feel like you’re thousands of kilometres away, in Punjab, India.
Tous deux hésitent à se faire photograph: Both hesitate to have their picture taken, then decide to show us their friendly smiles. “Why do you want our photo? We’re just normal people,” they say in Hindi. That is precisely what makes their stories so beautiful.
